subject: History
source: National Curriculum KS2 (the Roman Empire and its impact on Britain); no school Drive history material found for Y4, written from scratch | Spring 1 2027 (lessons 5 to 12): Tarbiyyah Primary Year 4 curriculum map and History Long Term Plan 2023-24 (Cornerstones Marvellous Medicine: medicine through time); TGA Year 4 pack

lessons.title: The Roman Empire and the invasion of Britain
objectives: Explain what the Roman Empire was
Describe why and when the Romans invaded Britain in AD 43

keywords.def: many lands and peoples ruled by one government or leader
the ruler of an empire
a large unit of the Roman army of about 5,000 soldiers
entering a country with an army to take control
the years counted forwards from the year 1

starter: Which age came before the Romans in Britain: Iron Age or Bronze Age?
Do BC numbers get bigger or smaller as we go forwards in time?

teach.heading: Bismillah: the Roman Empire
bullets: Rome began as a city in Italy
Its army conquered lands around the Mediterranean
By AD 117 it was at its largest
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Show a map of the Roman Empire at its largest extent (AD 117, under Trajan), covering North Africa, Egypt and the Middle East. Point out that Egypt and Syria were also Roman provinces.

teach.heading: A strong army
bullets: They trained hard and wore armour
teach.note: Show a picture of a legionary with a shield (scutum), helmet and short sword. Ask: how did discipline help them win battles?

teach.heading: Why invade Britain?
bullets: Britain had tin, lead, gold and grain
Emperor Claudius wanted fame and power
Some British tribes were helping Rome's enemies
teach.note: Be careful to present reasons as historians' explanations. Julius Caesar had visited Britain in 55 and 54 BC, but he did not stay.

teach.heading: AD 43: the invasion
bullets: About 40,000 Roman soldiers landed in Kent
They defeated tribes such as the Catuvellauni
The south of Britain soon became Roman
teach.note: The invasion in AD 43 was ordered by Claudius. Use 'about' for numbers. Many tribes were conquered over years, not days; ask why it took so long to control the whole island.

practice: What is an empire? Give a definition in your own words.
Name two reasons why the Romans invaded Britain.
In what year did the Roman invasion begin?
independent: Label a map of the Roman Empire with Rome, Britain and Egypt
Write four sentences: who, what, when, why of the invasion
Explain in a paragraph why Roman soldiers were so successful
exit: Which emperor sent the army to Britain in AD 43?
lessons.homework: Find three places in Britain with names that came from Roman times and note them down.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: map with places already marked and a word bank. Stretch: compare two reasons for invading and say which was most important.

lessons.title: Resistance: Boudica's rebellion
objectives: Describe how some Britons resisted Roman rule

keywords.def: fighting against those in power
a group of people with the same ruler and way of life
the tribe of eastern England led by Boudica
something that gives us information about the past

starter: In what year did the Romans invade Britain?
Name one reason the Romans wanted Britain.

teach.heading: Resistance to Rome
bullets: Some tribes made deals with Rome instead
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and a thought on justice and fairness. Not all Britons opposed Rome: some tribal kings became allies. Ask why.

teach.heading: Who was Boudica?
bullets: Boudica was queen of the Iceni
The Romans seized the Iceni lands
teach.note: Prasutagus left his kingdom to his daughters and the Roman emperor; Rome ignored this. Our main source is the Roman writer Tacitus, who wrote about 40 years later.

teach.heading: The rebellion, AD 60 or 61
bullets: They destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium
teach.note: Camulodunum is Colchester; Verulamium is near St Albans. Londinium was burnt: archaeologists still find a red layer of burnt earth in London. Keep it factual and avoid graphic detail.

teach.heading: The defeat
bullets: A Roman governor, Suetonius Paulinus, led the reply
teach.note: We do not know the exact location of the final battle. Ask: whose side of the story do we mostly read? Roman writers wrote our sources, so be careful about bias.

practice: Name two Roman towns that Boudica attacked.
Why must we be careful with Roman sources?
independent: Draw a map showing Iceni land and the three towns attacked
Write a diary entry from the point of view of an Iceni villager before the rebellion
Make a list of causes and consequences of the rebellion
exit: Who led the Iceni against the Romans?
Why is it hard to be sure about the Boudica story?
lessons.homework: Look for a statue or picture of Boudica and write two sentences about how the artist shows her.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: timeline cards for the rebellion to order. Stretch: judge whether the Roman sources about Boudica are fair, with one reason.

lessons.title: Roman roads, towns and Hadrian's Wall
objectives: Describe what Roman towns and roads were like
Explain why Hadrian's Wall was built

keywords.def: the Roman name for London
the central market and meeting place of a Roman town
a bridge or channel carrying water
the border of an empire or country

starter: Which Roman town was London called?
Why must we be careful with Roman sources?

teach.heading: Roman roads
bullets: Roads were straight and well built
Layers of stone and gravel drained water
Many modern roads follow Roman routes
teach.note: Bismillah. Explain that roads let soldiers and traders travel fast. Examples: Watling Street ran from the Kent coast to London and beyond. Ask: why straight?

teach.heading: Londinium and other towns
bullets: Londinium grew beside the River Thames
Towns had a forum, baths and temples
teach.note: Londinium was founded after AD 43 and became the main city of Roman Britain. Ask pupils who live in London what remains today, e.g. parts of the Roman wall near Tower Hill.

teach.heading: Roman baths
bullets: People met friends at the baths
Rooms were heated from beneath the floor
Bath had a famous hot spring
teach.note: Mention the baths at Aquae Sulis (Bath). Underfloor heating was called a hypocaust. Avoid claiming everyone could afford the baths; ask who might have been excluded.

teach.heading: Hadrian's Wall
bullets: It ran about 73 miles across northern Britain
Soldiers lived in forts along it
teach.note: Emperor Hadrian ordered it. It marked the northern frontier and controlled movement; ask: was it to keep people out or to control trade and taxes? Both ideas are suggested by historians.

practice: Why did the Romans build straight roads?
Name three buildings found in a Roman town.
Who ordered Hadrian's Wall to be built?
independent: Sketch a plan of a Roman town and label forum, baths and road
Explain in a paragraph why Hadrian's Wall was built
Locate Londinium and Hadrian's Wall on a map of Britain
exit: Name two things Roman towns had that Iron Age villages did not.
What was Hadrian's Wall built to do?
lessons.homework: Find one Roman road near where you live or in London and note its modern name.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: labelled town plan to complete with picture cards. Stretch: write two reasons for and two against the claim 'the Romans improved Britain'.

lessons.title: What did the Romans leave behind?
objectives: Identify Roman legacies in Britain today
Explain when and why the Romans left Britain

keywords.def: something that is passed down from the past to today
the language of the Romans
a large Roman country house with farmland
a picture made from tiny coloured tiles

starter: Name one thing a Roman road tells us about the Romans.

teach.heading: Roman legacy
bullets: Towns, baths and central heating ideas
Many of our months and numbers
teach.note: Bismillah. Ask pupils to guess what 'legacy' means from the picture of a gift handed down. Introduce months: January from Janus, July for Julius Caesar, August for Augustus.

teach.heading: Latin in English
bullets: Latin words in English: street, wall, port
Place names ending -chester or -caster mean fort
Roman numbers like XII are still used
teach.note: Latin 'strata' gave 'street'. Place names such as Manchester and Lancaster come from the Roman 'castra', meaning fort. Check pupils' own place names.

teach.heading: Villas and mosaics
bullets: Fishbourne Roman Palace has famous mosaics
teach.note: Show a mosaic picture. Ask what mosaics tell us about the people who owned them: wealthy, artistic, global trade. Islamic art also uses mosaic and tilework; this is a good link.

teach.heading: The Romans leave
bullets: The Romans left Britain around AD 410
The empire was under attack at home
teach.note: Emperor Honorius is said to have told Britons to look to their own defence in AD 410. Roman rule lasted about 400 years. Ask: what might Britain have been like when soldiers left?

practice: What does the word legacy mean?
Name two Roman legacies you can still see today.
Why did the Romans leave Britain?
independent: Create a leaflet 'The Romans: what they gave us'
Include at least four legacies with a sentence about each
Add a final sentence: the most important Roman legacy is ...
exit: Name one Roman legacy and explain it.
Around what year did the Romans leave?
lessons.homework: Find one Latin word or Roman number used in your home or neighbourhood and report back.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: leaflet template with pictures and sentence starters. Stretch: argue which legacy has lasted longest and why.

lessons.title: Healers and herbs: medicine long ago
lessons.bigQuestion: If you were ill 3,000 years ago, who would help you?
objectives: To understand how people in ancient times treated illness with herbs and healers
successCriteria: All: name one remedy people used long ago
Most: describe how ancient Egyptian and Greek healers treated illness
Some: explain why some old remedies worked
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: trusting Allah while seeking a cure

keywords.def: something used to treat an illness
a person who treats the sick
a plant used for flavour or medicine
100 years
watching carefully and noting what you see

hook.text: Why might honey have been used on cuts thousands of years ago?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: 'Allah has not sent down a disease except that He has also sent down its cure' (Sahih al-Bukhari). Allah also says of honey that in it is healing for people (an-Nahl 16:69). So Muslims have always looked for cures, while trusting Allah who gives health.

starter.q: How many years in a century?
BC dates come before or after AD dates?
Name one thing you do when you have a cold.
starter.a: For example: rest, drink water, take medicine

teach.heading: Being ill long ago
bullets: No hospitals as we know them
Families and healers cared for the sick
teach.note: Ask: what would you miss most if you were ill with no doctor or chemist?

teach.heading: Ancient Egypt
bullets: Some remedies were based on belief, not tests
teach.note: The Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BC) lists hundreds of remedies. Honey really does help keep wounds clean.

teach.heading: Ancient Greece: Hippocrates
teach.note: Hippocrates (about 460 to 370 BC) taught doctors to observe. The four humours idea was wrong, but careful observation was a big step.

teach.heading: Remedies through time
teach.note: Pupils vote on each before you reveal.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

options: Taught doctors to observe patients and look for natural causes
check.why: Germs were discovered much later. Hippocrates's big idea was careful observation.

practice.q: Name a remedy from ancient Egypt that really helped.
practice.a: Honey on wounds
practice.model:
Look at the Egypt slide.
Honey was put on cuts.
It keeps wounds clean, so it helped.

practice.q: What did Hippocrates teach doctors to do?
practice.a: Observe patients carefully and look for natural causes

practice.q: Willow bark was used for pain. What modern medicine is linked to it?
practice.a: Aspirin

independent.q: Core: Write three facts about healers long ago (one Egyptian, one Greek, one about herbs). Use the portal response box or your book.
independent.a: For example: Egyptians wrote remedies on papyrus; Hippocrates watched patients; willow bark eased pain
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 'Fact 1: Egyptian doctors put honey on wounds to keep them clean.'

independent.q: Extend: Why did some old remedies not work?
independent.a: They were based on wrong ideas, like charms or the four humours

independent.q: Stretch: Why was careful observation such a big step forward?
independent.a: Doctors could learn what really worked by watching what happened

exit.a: Something used to treat an illness
options: Something used to treat an illness

exit.q: Big question: if you were ill 3,000 years ago, who would help you?
exit.a: Family and healers, using herbs, honey and simple remedies

lessons.homework: Find three herbs or spices in your kitchen and ask an adult whether people use them to feel better.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards of remedies to sort. EAL: remedy, healer, herb with pictures. Stretch: find out what the Ebers Papyrus is.

lessons.title: How do we know? Sources about medicine in the Middle Ages
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we find out about medicine from 700 years ago?
objectives: To understand how historians use sources to learn about medieval medicine
successCriteria: All: name two kinds of historical source
Most: say what a source tells us about medieval medicine
Some: say what a source cannot tell us
lessons.smsc: Moral: checking information before we believe it

keywords.def: anything from the past that tells us about it
information that shows something is true
a place where monks lived and worked
a book about plants used as medicine
the Middle Ages, about 1000 to 1500

hook.text: If someone found your house in 700 years, what would tell them how you looked after a cold?

islamicLink.text: Islam teaches us to check news before we believe it. Allah says: if someone brings you news, verify it (al-Hujurat 49:6). Historians do the same with sources: they check them carefully before they trust them.

starter.a: Something used to treat an illness

teach.heading: Medicine in medieval England
bullets: Many still believed in the four humours
teach.note: Monasteries cared for the sick and grew herbs like sage and mint.

teach.heading: Kinds of source
teach.note: Ask pupils to sort into written and not written.

teach.heading: Reading a source
bullets: What does it not tell us?
teach.note: Model with a photo of a medieval herbal page (plants only): it tells us which plants were used; it does not tell us if they worked.

model.problem: What does a medieval herbal tell us?
steps: Who: written by a monk or healer
Tells us: which plants were used for which illnesses
Does not tell us: whether the remedies worked
model.answer: It shows what people believed helped, not whether it did.

teach.heading: Comparing sources
teach.note: If a herbal and a monastery garden plan both show sage, we can be more sure it was used.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.why: A herbal is written. Jars and gardens are sources too, but not written.

practice.q: A medieval medicine jar is found. Is it a source?
practice.a: Yes: an object source
practice.model:
Is it from the past? Yes.
Does it tell us something? Yes, that medicines were stored in jars.
So it is a source.

practice.q: Name one thing a herbal tells us.
practice.a: Which plants were used for which illnesses

practice.q: Name one thing a herbal cannot tell us.
practice.a: Whether the remedies worked

independent.q: Core: Look at the source cards. For each, write what it tells us about medieval medicine.
independent.a: Herbal: plants used; monastery garden: monks grew herbs; jar: medicines were stored; tools: surgery happened
independent.model: Teacher shows card 1: 'A monastery garden plan: tells us monks grew herbs like sage to treat the sick.'

independent.q: Extend: Which source is most useful and why?
independent.a: For example: the herbal, because it names plants and illnesses

independent.q: Stretch: Why should historians use more than one source?
independent.a: To check the facts and get a fuller picture

exit.a: Anything from the past that tells us about it
options: Anything from the past that tells us about it

exit.q: Big question: how can we find out about medicine from 700 years ago?
exit.a: By using sources: herbals, records, objects and places, and comparing them

lessons.homework: Find an object at home that a historian in the future could use as a source about health today.
lessons.send: SEND: source cards with picture and one-line caption. EAL: source, evidence, tells us. Stretch: think of one question a source cannot answer.

lessons.title: Muslim physicians: al-Razi and the first hospitals
lessons.bigQuestion: What made a good hospital 1,100 years ago?
objectives: To understand how Muslim physicians and hospitals advanced medicine
successCriteria: All: say who al-Razi was
Most: describe what a bimaristan was like
Some: explain why al-Razi's careful observation mattered
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for the sick, rich or poor

keywords.def: a doctor
a hospital in the Muslim world
a room in a hospital for patients
a deadly disease that caused spots and fever
a person who studies deeply

hook.text: If you built a hospital, what would it need to help people get better?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: 'Allah has not sent down a disease except that He has also sent down its cure' (Sahih al-Bukhari). Muslim rulers built hospitals that cared for everyone, rich or poor, because caring for the sick is a good deed. The Prophet, peace be upon him, told Muslims to visit the sick (Sahih al-Bukhari).

starter.q: Who taught doctors to observe patients?

starter.a: For example: a herbal, a jar, a building

teach.heading: Medicine in the Muslim world
bullets: Baghdad was a centre of learning
teach.note: In the 800s and 900s, scholars in Baghdad studied Greek medicine and tested it.

teach.heading: Al-Razi (about 854 to 925)
bullets: Ran hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad
teach.note: His encyclopedia is called al-Hawi. He wrote down what happened to each patient.

teach.heading: Smallpox and measles
bullets: Al-Razi wrote a book about them
He showed how to tell them apart
teach.note: This is one of the earliest clear descriptions of the two diseases.

teach.heading: The bimaristan
teach.note: Baghdad's al-Adudi hospital opened in about 982 with many doctors.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.why: Bimaristan is the Persian-origin word used for hospitals in the Muslim world.

practice.q: Where did al-Razi run hospitals?
practice.a: Rayy and Baghdad
practice.model:
Look at the al-Razi slide.
He ran hospitals in two cities.
Rayy and Baghdad.

practice.q: Which two diseases did al-Razi describe?
practice.a: Smallpox and measles

practice.q: Give one way a bimaristan was like a hospital today.
practice.a: For example: wards for different illnesses or a pharmacy

independent.q: Core: Write a fact file on al-Razi: when, where, what he did. Use the portal response box or your book.
independent.a: About 854 to 925; Rayy and Baghdad; ran hospitals, wrote al-Hawi, described smallpox and measles
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: 'Name: Abu Bakr al-Razi. Lived: about 854 to 925. Place: Rayy and Baghdad.'

independent.q: Extend: Describe a bimaristan in two sentences.
independent.a: For example: It had wards for different illnesses. Rich and poor were cared for.

independent.q: Stretch: Why does writing down each patient's illness help medicine improve?
independent.a: Doctors can compare cases and learn which treatments work

exit.q: Big question: what made a good hospital 1,100 years ago?
exit.a: Separate wards, trained doctors, a pharmacy and care for rich and poor, as in the bimaristans

lessons.homework: Design a floor plan for a bimaristan with wards, a pharmacy and a library (shapes and labels only).
lessons.send: SEND: fact file frame with picture prompts. EAL: physician, hospital, ward. Stretch: find out about another Muslim hospital, such as al-Nuri in Damascus.

lessons.title: Ibn Sina and The Canon of Medicine
lessons.bigQuestion: How could one book be used by doctors for 600 years?
objectives: To understand why Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was so important
successCriteria: All: say who Ibn Sina was and name his famous book
Most: describe two ideas in the Canon
Some: explain why the Canon spread to Europe
lessons.smsc: Cultural: the contribution of Muslim scholars to world medicine

keywords.def: a big book of rules and knowledge
a book used to teach a subject
change words into another language
able to spread from person to person
keeping sick people apart so illness does not spread

hook.text: If you wanted to share everything you knew with people 500 years from now, how would you do it?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught: if you hear of plague in a land, do not go there, and if it breaks out where you are, do not leave (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). This teaching about stopping illness spreading fits Ibn Sina's ideas about contagious disease.

starter.q: Name the city where al-Razi worked.

teach.heading: Ibn Sina (980 to 1037)
bullets: Wrote on medicine and many other subjects
teach.note: In Europe he became known as Avicenna.

teach.heading: The Canon of Medicine
teach.note: Its Arabic name is al-Qanun fi al-Tibb. It brought together Greek, Persian and Indian knowledge with his own.

teach.heading: Big ideas
bullets: Some diseases spread from person to person
teach.note: He gave rules for testing medicines: test on the illness it is meant for, and see if it works every time.

teach.heading: Spreading to Europe
teach.note: Gerard of Cremona translated it in Toledo. It was a main textbook in Europe until about the 1600s.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Why did the Canon spread across Europe?
check.why: Latin was the language of learning in Europe, so a Latin translation spread it.

practice.q: What is the Canon of Medicine?
practice.a: Ibn Sina's large book of medical knowledge
practice.model:
Read the title: The Canon of Medicine.
Canon means a big book of rules.
It is Ibn Sina's book of medical knowledge.

practice.q: Name one big idea in the Canon.
practice.a: For example: some diseases spread; test medicines carefully

practice.q: Into which language was it translated for Europe?
practice.a: Latin

independent.q: Core: Make a timeline of Ibn Sina's life with four dates and events.
independent.a: 980 born; about 1025 Canon finished; 1037 dies; 1100s Latin translation
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: line from 950 to 1200, mark 980 'born near Bukhara'.

independent.q: Extend: Write why the Canon was used for so long.
independent.a: It was clear, organised and full of tested knowledge, and it was translated so many could read it

independent.q: Stretch: How is Ibn Sina's idea about testing medicines like science today?
independent.a: Scientists still test medicines carefully and repeat tests to check they work

exit.q: Ibn Sina was known in Europe as:
Big question: how could one book be used by doctors for 600 years?
exit.a: It was clear and complete, and translated into Latin so European universities used it

lessons.homework: Teach a family member three facts about Ibn Sina.
lessons.send: SEND: timeline cards to order. EAL: book, translate, Europe. Stretch: research one other subject Ibn Sina wrote about.

lessons.title: Edward Jenner and the first vaccine
lessons.bigQuestion: How did a disease of cows help save millions of lives?
objectives: To understand how Edward Jenner developed vaccination against smallpox
successCriteria: All: say what Jenner discovered and when
Most: describe the steps of his experiment
Some: explain the link between variolation in Turkey and Jenner's work
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: how the body fights disease

keywords.def: a deadly disease with fever and spots
a mild disease caught from cows
giving a weak form of a disease to protect against it
the body's protection against a disease
an older way to protect people using material from mild smallpox

hook.text: Milkmaids rarely caught smallpox. If you noticed that, what would you want to find out?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: 'Allah has not sent down a disease except that He has also sent down its cure' (Sahih al-Bukhari). Vaccination is one way people found a cure Allah had placed in His creation. Many Muslim scholars have said that vaccines are a permitted way to protect health.

starter.a: Able to spread from person to person

teach.heading: Smallpox
teach.note: Be calm and factual. Smallpox killed many people across the world.

teach.heading: Variolation
bullets: Used in the Ottoman Empire and elsewhere
Lady Mary Wortley Montagu saw it in Istanbul
She brought it to England in 1721
teach.note: Variolation used material from mild smallpox. It worked but could be dangerous.

teach.heading: Jenner's experiment, 1796
bullets: Took cowpox from a milkmaid's sore
Put it into a boy, James Phipps
Later, smallpox did not affect him
teach.note: Jenner was a doctor in Berkeley, Gloucestershire. Ask: was it fair to test on a child? Today tests need strict permission.

teach.heading: A new word
teach.note: Ask: why was cowpox safer to use than smallpox?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Jenner used which disease to protect against smallpox?
check.why: Cowpox is mild and gave protection against smallpox.

practice.q: Put in order: test on James, notice milkmaids, result: no smallpox.
practice.a: Notice milkmaids, test on James, result: no smallpox
practice.model:
First Jenner noticed something.
Then he tested his idea.
Then he saw the result.

practice.q: In which year did Jenner test his idea?
Where did Lady Mary Wortley Montagu see variolation?
practice.a: In Istanbul, in the Ottoman Empire

independent.q: Core: Write the steps of Jenner's experiment as a numbered list.
independent.a: 1. Noticed milkmaids rarely caught smallpox. 2. Took cowpox from a milkmaid. 3. Put it into James Phipps. 4. Later gave him smallpox material. 5. He did not get ill.
independent.model: Teacher shows step 1: 'Jenner noticed that milkmaids who had cowpox did not catch smallpox.'

independent.q: Extend: Why was vaccination safer than variolation?
independent.a: It used mild cowpox, not smallpox, so it was less dangerous

independent.q: Stretch: Would Jenner's test be allowed today? Why?
independent.a: No: testing on a child without strict safety rules and permission would not be allowed

exit.q: Vaccine comes from the Latin word for:
Big question: how did a disease of cows help save millions of lives?
exit.a: Cowpox gave protection against smallpox, so Jenner made the first vaccine

lessons.homework: Ask an adult which vaccines you had as a baby (the red book may show them).
lessons.send: SEND: step cards with pictures to order. EAL: cow, disease, protect. Stretch: research how smallpox was ended worldwide.

lessons.title: How did vaccination change the world?
lessons.bigQuestion: Was the end of smallpox the greatest success in the history of medicine?
objectives: To understand the significance of vaccination from Jenner to today
successCriteria: All: say when smallpox was declared gone from the world
Most: describe one reason some people opposed vaccination
Some: judge how significant vaccination was, with reasons
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading a timeline with intervals
lessons.smsc: Moral: the value of every human life

keywords.def: important, with big effects
get rid of completely
something the law says you must do
people who are against something
the effect something has

hook.text: What would your life be like if there were no vaccines?

islamicLink.text: Allah says that whoever saves one life, it is as if he has saved all of mankind (al-Ma'idah 5:32). Ending smallpox saved countless lives, which shows how much good medicine can do.

starter.a: The body's protection against a disease

teach.heading: After Jenner
bullets: Britain made it compulsory for babies in 1853
teach.note: The Vaccination Act of 1853 made it compulsory for babies in England and Wales.

teach.heading: Opposition
bullets: Some disliked being told by law
teach.note: Show only the idea: people worried and some protested. Ask: why might people be scared of something new?

teach.heading: Smallpox eradicated
teach.note: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980. It is the only human disease ended this way.

teach.heading: Is it significant?
bullets: How many people did it affect?
How long did the effects last?
teach.note: Use the three questions as a test of significance.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.why: 1796 is Jenner's test; 1853 the Act; 1980 the declaration.

practice.q: Use the test: how many people did vaccination affect?
practice.a: Millions across the whole world
practice.model:
Ask: who did it help?
People in every country.
So it affected millions: very significant.

practice.q: Give one reason people opposed vaccination.
practice.a: Fear of something new, or not wanting the law to force them

practice.q: Does vaccination still matter today?
practice.a: Yes: babies and adults are still vaccinated against many diseases

independent.q: Core: Write a paragraph: 'Vaccination was significant because ...' Use the three tests. Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: For example: Vaccination was significant because it saved millions, its effects lasted, and it still protects us today
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: Point: Vaccination was very significant. Evidence: smallpox was eradicated in 1980. Explain: so no one dies of smallpox today.

independent.q: Extend: Add how Muslim and English history are linked in this story.
independent.a: Variolation was seen in the Ottoman Empire and brought to England in 1721, before Jenner

independent.q: Stretch: Was vaccination more significant than the bimaristan? Give a reason.
independent.a: Any reasoned answer, for example: yes, because it ended a disease worldwide

exit.q: Big question: was the end of smallpox the greatest success in the history of medicine?
exit.a: Reasoned answer using the significance tests

lessons.homework: Make a short 'medicine through time' quiz of five questions for your family.
lessons.send: SEND: paragraph frame with the three tests. EAL: important because ... Stretch: write both a 'for' and an 'against' sentence before your view.

lessons.title: Florence Nightingale and clean hospitals
lessons.bigQuestion: How can cleaning a hospital save more lives than a new medicine?
objectives: To understand how Florence Nightingale improved nursing and hospital hygiene
successCriteria: All: say where and when Florence Nightingale worked
Most: describe two changes she made at Scutari
Some: explain how she used numbers to persuade people
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: using statistics to show facts
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for others through hard work

keywords.def: a person trained to care for the sick
keeping clean to stop disease
a war fought in the 1850s near the Black Sea
numbers collected to show facts
one of the first to do something

hook.text: A hospital is dirty and crowded. What three things would you change first?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said that purity is half of faith (Sahih Muslim). Muslims wash before every prayer. Nightingale showed that cleanliness saves lives in hospitals too.

teach.heading: The Crimean War
bullets: Wounded soldiers sent to Scutari, near Istanbul
The hospital was dirty and crowded
teach.note: More soldiers died from disease than from wounds.

teach.heading: Florence Nightingale (1820 to 1910)
bullets: Came with a team of nurses
teach.note: Show the barracks building at Scutari (Selimiye Barracks) that became the hospital.

teach.heading: What she changed
teach.note: A government team also fixed the drains in 1855. Together, deaths fell sharply.

teach.heading: Numbers that persuade
bullets: Drew diagrams of causes of death
Showed disease was the biggest killer
teach.note: Her diagrams helped persuade the government to improve army hospitals. In 1860 she opened a nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital, London.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: At Scutari, most soldiers died from:
check.why: Disease killed more soldiers than wounds, which is why cleanliness mattered so much.

practice.q: Where was the Scutari hospital?
practice.a: Near Istanbul (in today's Turkey)
practice.model:
Read the first slide.
Scutari is near Istanbul.
So the hospital was near Istanbul.

practice.q: Name two changes Nightingale made.
practice.a: For example: cleaned the wards and gave better food

practice.q: Why did she collect statistics?
practice.a: To show disease was killing soldiers and persuade the government to act

independent.q: Core: Make a before-and-after table for the hospital at Scutari (three rows).
independent.a: Dirty wards / cleaned; poor food / good food; no clean linen / laundry organised
independent.model: Teacher shows row 1: 'Before: dirty wards. After: wards scrubbed clean.'

independent.q: Extend: Write one sentence on why she is called a pioneer.
independent.a: She was one of the first to train nurses and use statistics to improve hospitals

independent.q: Stretch: How is Nightingale's work linked to the bimaristan idea?
independent.a: Both believed in clean, organised hospitals with trained staff

exit.q: Big question: how can cleaning a hospital save more lives than a new medicine?
exit.a: Dirt spreads disease; cleaning stops infections, so fewer people die

lessons.homework: Make a hygiene poster for your home with three rules for stopping germs spreading.
lessons.send: SEND: before-and-after picture cards. EAL: clean, dirty, before, after. Stretch: sketch two bars (disease, wounds) to show which killed more soldiers, with no numbers needed.

lessons.title: Mary Seacole: courage and care
lessons.bigQuestion: Should Mary Seacole be remembered as much as Florence Nightingale?
objectives: To understand Mary Seacole's work in the Crimean War and compare her with Florence Nightingale
successCriteria: All: say who Mary Seacole was
Most: compare Seacole and Nightingale in two ways
Some: judge how significant each was, with evidence
lessons.smsc: Moral: perseverance and courage in doing good

keywords.def: an island in the Caribbean Sea
the place Seacole built near the battlefront
a book someone writes about their own life
how important someone or something is
say what is the same and different

hook.text: If you were turned away when you offered to help, what would you do next?

islamicLink.text: Allah loves those who do good (al-Baqarah 2:195). Mary Seacole did not give up when she was turned away; she found another way to help. Doing good with courage is something Islam praises.

starter.q: At Scutari most soldiers died from:
Nightingale opened a nursing school in which year?

teach.heading: Mary Seacole (1805 to 1881)
teach.note: Her mother kept a boarding house and used herbal remedies.

teach.heading: Going to the war
bullets: Paid her own way to the Crimea
teach.note: Ask: what does this tell us about her character?

teach.heading: The British Hotel, 1855
bullets: Food, rest and medicines for soldiers
Went to the battlefield to help
teach.note: She also cared for wounded soldiers near the fighting. She wrote an autobiography in 1857.

teach.heading: Two women, one war
teach.note: Pupils add a point to each side.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: How did Mary Seacole get to the Crimea?
check.why: She was not chosen, so she travelled at her own cost.

practice.q: Where was Mary Seacole born?
practice.a: Kingston, Jamaica
practice.model:
Look at the first slide.
She was born in Kingston.
Kingston is in Jamaica.

practice.q: What was the British Hotel?
practice.a: A place near the front that gave soldiers food, rest and medicines

practice.q: Give one way Seacole and Nightingale were similar.
practice.a: Both cared for soldiers in the Crimean War

independent.q: Core: Complete a comparison table: where they worked, how they got there, what they did, what they are remembered for.
independent.a: Nightingale: Scutari, sent with nurses, cleaned hospital, nursing and statistics. Seacole: near Balaclava, own money, British Hotel and battlefield care, courage
independent.model: Teacher shows row 1: 'Where: Nightingale at Scutari hospital; Seacole near Balaclava.'

independent.q: Extend: Write a paragraph answering the big question. Use the portal response box.
independent.a: For example: Yes, because she showed great courage and helped soldiers near the front, though Nightingale changed nursing for the long term

independent.q: Stretch: Why might Seacole have been forgotten for many years and remembered again later?
independent.a: Her work was less official and recorded; later historians looked again at her autobiography

exit.q: Seacole wrote about her life in an:
Big question: should Mary Seacole be remembered as much as Florence Nightingale?
exit.a: Reasoned view with evidence about each woman's work
